why.text: The only hard anchor is China's official foreign-exchange reserves, which SAFE publishes: $3,400.3bn at the end of September 2026. SAFE IC invests part of them, and nobody outside publishes how much.

sources.name: People's Daily / Xinhua: China's FX reserves, end-September 2026

why.text: The two ends of the range are two different shares of that anchor. A third of reserves is about $1,133bn ($3,400.3bn ÷ 3); the press estimate quoted a third of the $3,227bn reserves of the time. Global SWF's $2,047bn is about 60% of today's reserves ($2,047bn ÷ $3,400.3bn). We could not find Global SWF's fund-level method, so we cannot show how it got there.

We could not use US filings. SAFE IC does not appear in SEC Form 13F filings: a full-text search of EDGAR for 13F-HR filings naming "SAFE Investment" returned no results. US Treasury data shows mainland China holding $590.7bn and Hong Kong $261.5bn of US Treasuries at the end of August 2026, but those are country totals, not SAFE IC's.

why.text: The Government declines to publish GIC's size. Its reason: with the figures for MAS and Temasek already public, GIC's number would give away the size of the reserves as a whole.

sources.name: Singapore MOF: what are Singapore's reserves?

why.text: The budget gives a cross-check, and it fails for sizing GIC. The Net Investment Returns Contribution (NIRC) is S$28.5bn in FY2026. It is up to 50% of the expected long-term real return on the net assets of GIC, MAS and Temasek minus the Government's own liabilities, plus up to 50% of investment income on the remaining reserves. The expected return rate is not published. As an illustration only: if the whole NIRC were half of a 4% real return (our assumption), the net pool would be about S$1.4tn. MAS (S$551bn, June 2026) and Temasek (about S$518bn) are published and add up to about S$1.07tn, which would leave about S$0.36tn for GIC, far below the estimates above. The gap exists because the base is net of Government liabilities and the rate is assumed, so the budget cannot back GIC's size out.

sources.name: Singapore MOF: Net Investment Returns Contribution
Vulcan Post: MAS and Temasek figures

why.text: So the figure stays a third-party estimate. We show the budget arithmetic so you can see why it cannot replace one.

detail.summary: KIA does not publish its size; its law bars public statements about invested funds. Press estimates have risen from about $846bn to about $1,072bn in under two years.

source.name: Reuters: Gulf sovereign wealth funds were built for a rainy day

why.text: KIA manages two pools: the General Reserve Fund and the Future Generations Fund. Article 8 of Law 47 of 1982 bars public statements on invested funds, so KIA reports to the Council of Ministers and to a closed session of the National Assembly, not to the public.

The budget route is the obvious one. The Future Generations Fund was seeded in 1976 with half of the reserve fund and, for decades, took at least 10% of state revenue each year, with its income reinvested and withdrawals needing a law. Since Law 18 of 2020 the transfer depends on a budget surplus. That is a rule, not a record: we found no published series of the actual yearly transfers to add up.
Even with that series, transfers alone would understate the fund, because 50 years of reinvested returns sit on top. So the figure here stays a third-party estimate.

detail.cant: The yearly transfers into the Future Generations Fund, the split between the two funds, and any KIA-published total.

why.text: ADQ's audited accounts show total assets of AED 996,777m at the end of 2025 (AED 921,741m a year earlier). Divided by the 3.6725 dirham peg, that is about $271bn. The assets now sit under L'imad, so this is the closest audited anchor.

L'imad's own assets come on top. One is a 42.54% stake in Modon Holding, bought from IHC in October 2025. Global SWF's $300bn is about $29bn above ADQ's balance sheet, which is the right order of magnitude for that addition, but L'imad does not publish the value of its pre-merger assets, so we cannot reproduce the $300bn.

detail.title: The $1 trillion figure, explained
detail.summary: Danantara's official $1 trillion and Global SWF's $230bn measure different things. This page uses the official figure and shows the others.

source.name: Danantara press release, President Prabowo at WEF 2026

range.label: Global SWF: value of the stakes seeded into it
Total assets of the seven founding SOEs, from their published statements

source.name: Kontan: 7 BUMN Danantara, from the companies' published financial statements

why.text: The gap is about definition, not arithmetic. The official $1 trillion counts the assets of the state companies Danantara supervises. Global SWF counts what Danantara directly holds: it values the stakes handed to it at $172bn and says its figure contradicts media and government announcements. The Rp9,353tn figure is a third view: the combined total assets of the seven big SOEs first placed under Danantara.

We show the official figure as the headline because it is the only one published by Danantara, and we label it rounded. A direct-holdings figure would be the better measure of a fund's size, and Danantara has not published one.

detail.cant: Danantara's audited balance sheet, and the value of the stakes it directly holds. The Rp9,353tn total is company assets, not Danantara's stakes, and we have not converted it to dollars.
